Monday, week 2. Marco Bianchi replied to your memo:

Subject: Good work — here's where I want to go next

Oliver,

This is exactly the kind of memo I needed — it separates real findings from artifacts, which is rarer than it should be. A few reactions and where I want to push next week.

The lapsed-subscriber giveaway (~€57k) is now the headline for Tobias, not the promo/coupon story — good catch pulling it out. Before I take that number upstairs, I want it airtight. And the Welcome10 broad refund pattern is the one piece of "margin erosion" I think is genuinely actionable rather than a sample-size illusion, so I want to go a layer deeper there before we talk about capping anything.

On incrementality — I accept we may never get a clean causal answer here, but I'd like one more honest attempt before I write it off as "probably just bigger carts clear the threshold anyway."

Questions for this week:

1. **Is the active-but-orphan 18% a timing bug or a real gap?** I need to know whether the full €57k-ish exposure is confirmed leakage or whether part of it shrinks once the overlap check is fixed properly.

2. **What's actually driving Welcome10's refund pattern?** Is it concentrated in particular products, categories, or merchants, or does it look like people discount-shopping and then returning — i.e., is this a fit/expectation problem or a "discount attracts returners" problem?

3. **Can we get a cleaner incrementality read by comparing similar-sized orders with and without the discount**, rather than comparing discounted vs. all orders? I'd rather have a more honest "we still can't tell" than a flattering but confounded number.

4. **For the lapsed-subscriber leakage, how far back does it go and is it accelerating or steady?** I want to know if this is a slow-burning historical gap or something that's gotten worse recently, since that changes how urgently we need to fix the underlying process versus just write off the past.

No need to re-litigate the B2B volume-tier outlier — just keep it excluded as you planned. Let's talk Wednesday before the last batch so I can steer based on what the orphan-subscription check turns up.

Thanks,
Marco

Last week in the company's analytics channel:
- Chief Executive Officer team (Hannah Brooks): Revenue concentration: our top 5 merchants generate 72% of Tidewick's processing-fee revenue, and one merchant alone (Cragsley Outfitters) accounts for 42% — we're exposed if a top account leaves.
- Chief Executive Officer team (Hannah Brooks): Growth is healthy but comes from existing merchants: active merchants grew from 76 to 111 and orders roughly doubled over 2 years, yet new merchants contribute under 1% of revenue in their first quarter after joining.
- Chief Executive Officer team (Hannah Brooks): Refund rate is creeping up: from ~9-11% in 2024 to 12-14% in late 2025, without a matching rise in payment failures — worth a root-cause look.
- Chief Financial Officer team (Kofi Mensah): 2025 processing-fee revenue: Tidewick earned €93,583 in payment-processing fees on €3.97M of merchant payment volume, growing to a €14.3k December peak — full platform-fee revenue isn't in this data yet, to follow.
- Chief Financial Officer team (Kofi Mensah): Merchant concentration: our top 10 merchants still drive ~65% of payment volume (led by Cragsley Outfitters at ~18%), but that share is edging down as the merchant base grows (92 → 113 active merchants year over year).
- Chief Financial Officer team (Kofi Mensah): Refunds: Apparel merchants run a steady ~20% refund rate (normal for fashion), but a handful of smaller non-Apparel merchants (e.g. OfficeHub Nordic, Sports & Outdoor sellers) drove a refund-rate spike to ~13% company-wide in Q3 — still being double-checked against return records.
- Chief Operating Officer team (Lena Hartmann): Delivery speed held up over the past two years (~85-90% of orders arrive within 5 days in a normal month), but it took a real hit during peak season: only 56% of orders arrived within 5 days in the worst week (early December), before recovering within about 2 weeks.
- Chief Operating Officer team (Lena Hartmann): One of our carrier partners, Albion Parcel, broke down starting in November: on-time delivery (within 3 days) fell from 76% in October to 28% in November and December, and hasn't recovered yet.
- Chief Operating Officer team (Lena Hartmann): Which merchant has 'good' or 'bad' delivery isn't really about the merchant or the warehouse - it's almost entirely about which carrier handles their shipments: the exact same merchant sees 89% of parcels arrive within 3 days on one carrier vs. just 19% on another.
- VP Customer Experience team (Mateo Ruiz): Slower support replies mean unhappier customers: satisfaction drops from 4.4/5 when resolved in under 4 hours to just 1.7/5 when it takes more than 3 days.
- VP Customer Experience team (Mateo Ruiz): A big chunk of support tickets (~65% recently) are shoppers asking "where's my order" - and this spikes every November/December, matching a rise in late deliveries from ~4% to ~10%+ of shipments.
- VP Customer Experience team (Mateo Ruiz): One merchant's May 2025 delivery breakdown (70% of shipments took over a week, vs. under 5% normally) explains an unusual mid-year spike in slow support - it was a local incident, not a platform-wide issue.
- Head of Growth Marketing team (Sofie Nilsen): Discount codes are costing more than they earn in our core retail categories: discounted orders return 5-7 points more often than full-price ones (e.g. apparel 39% vs 35%, electronics 17% vs 11%), with no real boost in order size.
- Head of Growth Marketing team (Sofie Nilsen): Referral customers are our most engaged shoppers by far — people who refer others place ~8 orders/year vs ~3 for everyone else — while our loyalty program shows no such lift despite similar effort to run.
- Head of Growth Marketing team (Sofie Nilsen): Growth is concentrated: just 2 of our ~120 merchants generate 31% of all "direct" site traffic, and only 1 in 7 orders can be traced back to a marketing channel at all.
- Head of Merchant Success team (Arjun Patel): Our biggest merchant, Cragsley Outfitters, grew sales +19.8% year-over-year this holiday quarter (vs. the same Oct-Dec period last year) - real growth, not just seasonal bump.
- Head of Merchant Success team (Arjun Patel): Castell Fasteners, one of our top 4 merchants, is flashing a warning sign: shopper traffic on its site dropped 44% this quarter and it's sitting on €5,080 in unpaid invoices.
- Head of Merchant Success team (Arjun Patel): Merchants with naturally recurring purchases (coffee/food subscriptions, B2B restocking) keep 83-94% of customers coming back, vs. ~58% for general retail - a strong case for building reorder habits into any merchant's playbook.
- Head of Risk and Payments team (Claire Dubois): Access control: we can show who has access today, but we found zero audit records of role/permission changes over 3 years — so we can't yet prove when access was granted or revoked.
- Head of Risk and Payments team (Claire Dubois): Data privacy requests: all healthy — ~48 requests since 2023, with a consistent 30-day response window and no real backlog.
- Head of Risk and Payments team (Claire Dubois): Login security: one sharp anomaly — in Feb 2025, 61% of login attempts failed (7,429 of 12,211), a 10x jump from the normal ~6% baseline, and it wasn't flagged by our suspicious-access alerts at the time.
- VP Product team (Emeka Obi): 🛒 Most lost sales leak at the shopping cart, not at payment: only ~1 in 4 carts convert within an hour, and the rest mostly stall for 1-7 days before fizzling out (just 1-19% of those convert) — payment itself works fine once an order is actually placed (97.6% succeed instantly).
- VP Product team (Emeka Obi): 🔁 Most first-time buyers do come back: 40-62% of new customers place a second order within 90 days, typically within 1-2.5 months — a healthy, stable repeat-purchase baseline across the last 3 years.
- VP Product team (Emeka Obi): 📦 A return modestly cools the relationship but doesn't end it: customers with a returned order come back 49.7% of the time within 90 days, vs 57.7% for customers with no return — about an 8-point dip, not a cliff.
- Head of Data team (Yuki Tanaka): Revenue checks out: once you count refunded payments correctly, orders match actual money collected to within 1-5% (not the 20-40% gap it looked like at first).
- Head of Data team (Yuki Tanaka): Refunds are real and not lost or double-counted, but most (85%) land ~3 weeks after the original payout already went out, so we currently can't point to exactly which payout absorbed a given refund.
- Head of Data team (Yuki Tanaka): "How many customers do we have" depends entirely on definition: 11,258 total accounts, but only 6,159 bought in the last 12 months and just 411 have an active subscription — we recommend standardizing on the 6,159 figure as "active customers."
- Chief Information Security Officer team (Noah Fischer): 🔐 Shopper accounts have 0% multi-factor authentication (MFA) enabled — literally none of our ~11,200 shopper logins use a second factor, vs. ~55% of staff.
- Chief Information Security Officer team (Noah Fischer): 🕵️ We can't currently prove who deleted things: of 615 products deleted across 91 merchants, 0 show up in our audit log as a logged deletion.
- Chief Information Security Officer team (Noah Fischer): 👋 When a merchant churns, their staff logins don't get shut off: 16 Owner/Admin accounts on churned merchants are still marked "active," some unused for 500+ days.
- Data Protection Officer team (Priyanka Desai): 🔒 Privacy audit: our email-retention rule (delete after 730 days) is configured for all 120 merchants but has never actually run — we're still holding ~44,000+ customer emails that are over 2 years old.
- Data Protection Officer team (Priyanka Desai): ⚖️ 3 shoppers' erasure requests were correctly put on hold for payment disputes, but those holds are now 289–954 days old (up to 2.6 years) and need review before we can say the requests are truly resolved.
- Data Protection Officer team (Priyanka Desai): 📉 Marketing-email opt-in rate has slipped from 99.4% to ~90% since 2023, with a sharp spike in opt-outs in July–August 2025 — worth watching if we rely on consent for marketing.
- VP Platform Engineering team (Lucas Moreau): Background jobs ran reliably almost all of Q4 2025, except one bug in our cart-reminder emails that failed for a single week (Nov 24) and hit 10 merchants — including our #1 merchant by revenue, Cragsley Outfitters.
- VP Platform Engineering team (Lucas Moreau): About 1 in 7 webhook notifications we send to merchants' inventory/accounting systems (ERP, WMS, and Accounting syncs) never go through — they get stuck retrying instead of succeeding or failing cleanly, all year round.
- VP Platform Engineering team (Lucas Moreau): Support tickets roughly doubled for everyone over the holidays, but the 10 merchants hit by the cart-reminder bug saw tickets rise even more (+174% vs +148% for everyone else) — a real but modest extra hit on top of the seasonal spike.
- Head of Merchandising team (Zara Ahmed): Quality tail at a top merchant: 1 in 5 reviewed products (23 of 105) at Cragsley Outfitters, our #2 merchant by revenue, average below 3 stars — some still sell hundreds of units, so it's a brewing risk, not yet a sales problem.
- Head of Merchandising team (Zara Ahmed): Bundles are a missed opportunity: none of our top 6 merchants by revenue use product bundles at all (0% of their catalog), while curated collections are already used by 65-100% of merchants' products.
- Head of Merchandising team (Zara Ahmed): December 2025 saw the worst customer ratings in 3 years (3.71 avg, 1 in 4 reviews 1-2 stars) — traced mainly to two Home & Living merchants, not a platform-wide quality problem.
- Head of Pricing and Promotions team (Oliver Grant): Free subscription-box deliveries are going to already-canceled customers: 82% of orphaned 'free delivery' orders belong to customers who canceled an average of 117 days earlier (~€57k given away).
- Head of Pricing and Promotions team (Oliver Grant): No coupon in our system has any usage or per-customer limit set — repeat use of codes isn't a rule violation because no rule exists.
- Head of Pricing and Promotions team (Oliver Grant): Welcome10 orders run ~2x bigger than normal, but its refunds (€12.2k, spread across 92 separate returns) now exceed the discount's own cost.
- Head of Lifecycle Marketing team (Ingrid Solberg): Loyalty programme payout check: points redeemed by members cost us 19.4% of the revenue those members bring in (€177.8k redeemed vs €915k revenue) — a high "discount rate" for a rewards programme, with another €669k in issued-but-unredeemed points still owed.
- Head of Lifecycle Marketing team (Ingrid Solberg): Correcting an early red flag: loyalty members don't actually return items more than other customers once you compare like-for-like by product category — the earlier "members refund 2x more" number was mostly because members are concentrated in our highest-return category (apparel, ~38% refund rate for everyone there), not because membership itself drives returns.
- Head of Lifecycle Marketing team (Ingrid Solberg): Programme reach is small and uneven: only ~16% of customers are enrolled in loyalty (flat for 2 years), under 1% have ever used a referral code, and our B2B wholesale merchants have no loyalty programme at all.
- Head of B2B Commerce team (Daniel Kim): Lost B2B wholesale deals take ~4x longer to close than won ones (35.5 vs 9.1 days avg) — time-open is our clearest warning sign.
- Head of B2B Commerce team (Daniel Kim): Deal size doesn't predict win/loss: win rates stay flat at 79-88% across all deal-size bands, from under €3,000 to over €12,000.
- Head of B2B Commerce team (Daniel Kim): Performance is broadly consistent across our 5 B2B wholesale merchants (75-88% win rate), but one rep at Polder Packaging wins only 57% — a likely coaching opportunity, not a systemic issue.
- Director of Fulfilment Operations team (Fatima Zahra): Inventory accuracy: ongoing stock miscounts are small but rising — about 850 single-unit discrepancies/month in pick locations, up 24% since January (now ~940/month), worth roughly €20-25k/month.
- Director of Fulfilment Operations team (Fatima Zahra): It's a picking/process issue, not a tracking-tech issue: mismatches cluster heavily in high-SKU apparel/footwear lines, while items tracked by lot or serial number (food, appliances) actually show fewer discrepancies per unit sold.
- Director of Fulfilment Operations team (Fatima Zahra): A separate one-time ~€138k year-end stock correction on Dec 31 was ~94% concentrated in just 5 B2B wholesale merchants (office/industrial supplies) — likely an annual stocktake true-up, being confirmed with ops before we treat it as a trend.
- Support Operations Manager team (Ben Carter): We miss our own support SLA more often than we'd like: in 2025, 38% of tickets got a late first reply and 20% were resolved late — urgent tickets fared worst, missing resolution half the time (50.6%).
- Support Operations Manager team (Ben Carter): Customer happiness tracks almost perfectly with speed: average satisfaction drops from 4.4/5 on tickets resolved within 4 hours to 1.7/5 on tickets that take over a week — so faster replies are the single biggest lever on CSAT.
- Support Operations Manager team (Ben Carter): Support pain is concentrated, not spread evenly: just 3 of our ~94 merchants (Cragsley Outfitters, Marrowby & Vane, Studio Vrij) generate 34% of all support tickets, and these same merchants have the worst response times in the whole book.

- Head of Risk and Payments team (Claire Dubois): Login security: one sharp anomaly — in Feb 2025, 61% of login attempts failed (7,429 of 12,211), a 10x jump from the normal ~6% baseline, and it wasn't flagged by our suspicious-access alerts at the time.

input.notes:
Marco wants the €57k lapsed-subscriber number airtight before it goes to Tobias, wants Welcome10's refund pattern explained one layer deeper, wants an honest size-matched incrementality attempt, and wants the leakage trend over time — four questions, three slots tonight, so I'm sequencing by what's blocking the Wednesday sync.

Priority tonight is the subscription-leakage story since Marco explicitly wants it checked before taking it upstairs, so two of three slots go there:
1. A methodology check on the 18%/€11.7k "active" bucket from last week — I suspect this isn't a real gap but an artifact of how I categorized customers by their *single most-recent* subscription record: if their current subscription started after the free order, there may well have been an older (now-superseded) subscription that actually covered the order date, which would mean it belongs with the "canceled/lapsed" leakage story rather than being unexplained. I want this resolved before stating a number to Tobias.
2. A monthly trend (full 2023-2025 history) on the confirmed "canceled-subscriber" leakage bucket, to tell Marco whether this is a slow-burning historical gap or getting worse — directly answers his accelerating-or-steady question.

Third slot goes to digging one layer into Welcome10's refund pattern (which category of products it clusters in, and whether return timing looks like fit/expectation mismatch vs. quick-flip behavior) — the one piece Marco called out as worth a deeper look before any capping conversation. I'm holding the harder, size-matched incrementality re-cut for night 2, since it needs more careful design and isn't needed before Wednesday's sync, whereas the subscription-leakage number is.

Also noting for context (not acting on tonight): Growth Marketing's company-wide finding that discounted orders return 5-7pts more with no basket-size boost in apparel/electronics lines up with our Welcome10 finding — useful external corroboration, not a new data pull.

requests.title: Is the 'active' 18% of orphan subscription-delivery orders a categorization artifact or a real gap?
requests.question: For the ~291 orphan free-delivery orders where the customer's most-recent subscription record shows status 'active', did that order actually fall in a gap between an earlier (now-superseded) subscription and the current one, which would mean it belongs with the confirmed 'canceled' leakage group rather than being a separate unexplained case?
requests.grain: one row per explanation category
columns: category: 'order preceded customer's first-ever subscription' / 'order fell between two subscription stints (an older subscription record exists with started_at <= order date)' / 'unexplained - active subscription dates should already have overlapped'
requests.details: Source: start from the exact orphan-order population used in last week's reports (order_discounts + discounts name='Subscription delivery (prepaid)' + orders placed_at in 2025, status != 'cancelled', no overlapping subscription with status in trialing/active/past_due for that user+tenant), restricted to the subset whose most-recent subscription (by started_at) has status = 'active' (the 291-order/60-customer group from last week, ~€11,746). For each such order, check: (a) does the customer have any OTHER subscription row for that tenant (any status) with started_at <= order.placed_at? If yes and that older subscription's own coverage (started_at to ended_at, or started_at to current date if still open) does not include placed_at, classify as 'fell between two subscription stints'. If no such older row exists at all, classify as 'preceded first-ever subscription'. Otherwise ('unexplained') flag for manual review. Convert discount amounts to EUR via exchange_rates (base_code='EUR', quote_code=currency_code, as_of=placed_at). Order by order count descending. Print all categories (expect 3 rows).
builds_on: Subscription status distribution behind orphan comped-delivery orders

requests.title: Monthly trend of confirmed lapsed-subscriber free-delivery leakage, 2023-2025
requests.question: Is the confirmed leakage (free deliveries going to customers whose subscription had already been canceled) a slow-burning historical gap, steady, or accelerating?
requests.grain: one row per calendar month, 2023-01 through 2025-12
columns: orphan orders where most-recent subscription status = 'canceled' (count)
cumulative total discount amount, running sum since 2023-01 (EUR)
requests.details: Source: order_discounts + discounts (name='Subscription delivery (prepaid)') + orders (placed_at across full history 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31, status != 'cancelled', user_id, tenant_id) restricted to orders with no overlapping subscription (status in trialing/active/past_due, same overlap definition as before) AND whose customer's most-recent subscription (by started_at) has status = 'canceled' (the confirmed-leakage group, ~82% of orphans, ~€57k in 2025 alone). Join to calendar_days (or extract month from placed_at) to get month_label. Convert discount amounts to EUR via exchange_rates (base_code='EUR', quote_code=currency_code, as_of=placed_at). Order by month ascending. Print all 36 months.
builds_on: Subscription-delivery discount orders with no overlapping active subscription

requests.title: What's driving Welcome10's elevated refund pattern: category concentration and return timing
requests.question: Is the Welcome10 instance's outsized refund total concentrated in particular product categories, and does the time between order and return look like a fit/expectation-mismatch problem (fast returns) or something else?
requests.grain: one row per product category, restricted to the single Welcome10 discount instance with 260 orders (coupon_code='WELCOME10') identified in last week's report
columns: order_item count sold under this discount instance
return rate (% of items sold that were returned)
total refund amount for this category (EUR)
this category's share of the instance's total refund amount (%)
avg days between order placed_at and the return's requested_at (for returned items)
requests.details: Source: re-identify the same discount_id as last week by discounts.name='Welcome 10% off' whose 2025 non-cancelled order count via order_discounts equals exactly 260. For those 260 orders, join order_items (quantity, product_variant_id) -> product_variants -> products (primary_category_id) -> categories (name); join return_items (via order_item_id) -> order_returns (status, requested_at, refund_amount or order_returns.refund_total apportioned) for returns tied to those order_items. Convert refund amounts to EUR via exchange_rates (base_code='EUR', quote_code=currency_code, as_of=order_returns.requested_at or refunded_at). Order by total refund amount (EUR) descending, category name as tie-break. Print all categories.
builds_on: Concentration of refund cost on the two highest refund-to-discount-ratio instances

input.notes:
Night 1 raised one real problem and gave two solid answers:

Report 1 (the 'active' bucket breakdown) came back broken: only 1 of the 3 categories printed (88 orders, 30.2%), leaving 203 of the 291 orders unaccounted for entirely rather than showing 0-count rows. That smells like an inner-join dropping orders that had no matching 'older subscription' row — i.e. the 'preceded first-ever subscription' case was silently excluded rather than counted as zero. I can't hand Marco a number built on a query that's missing 70% of its own population, so this is priority one tonight: re-run with explicit NOT EXISTS/LEFT JOIN logic and a self-check total that must sum to 291.

Report 2 is a genuinely good, clean answer to Marco's trend question: leakage rose from ~€200/month in 2023 to a 2024 peak (~€2,000-3,300/month, Feb-Oct 2024), then has declined every month since, down to €819 in Nov 2025 and €0 in Dec 2025. This is the opposite of accelerating — it looks like a historical, now-shrinking gap. I want one more cut — by tenant — before I tell Marco it's broadly resolved, in case the decline is really just one or two tenants fixing something while others stay flat (which would change the "how urgent" answer).

Report 3 (Welcome10 drivers) shows returns spread across many apparel/footwear categories (Outerwear and Boots are the largest single contributors but no runaway concentration), with 9-19 day order-to-return gaps — consistent with normal apparel fit/try-and-return behavior, not quick-flip abuse. Combined with last week's finding that this instance's return rate is only +2.3pp above this tenant's own baseline (which is already ~37%), I think the right framing is shifting: refund-exceeding-discount-cost looks largely mechanical for any % discount at a high-baseline-return apparel merchant, not something the coupon itself is causing. I don't think this needs another report — I'll fold it into the memo with that caveat.

Tonight's three slots: (1) fix the broken categorization query, (2) the size-matched incrementality re-cut Marco asked for, (3) a tenant-level cut of the leakage trend to confirm the decline is broad-based before I call it resolved.

Night 2's categorization fix produced a clean but puzzling result: all 291 active-bucket orders now land in a single "unexplained" category (100%, €11,746.39) — meaning none of them precede a first subscription and none fall between two stints. Logically that leaves only one explanation: the "active" subscription record itself doesn't actually cover the order date (otherwise the order wouldn't have been flagged as orphan in the first place), which most likely means either (a) that subscription started *after* the free order — a different, more benign situation than leakage — or (b) the subscription is marked status='active' but already has a past ended_at on it, a genuine data inconsistency where the status field disagrees with the subscription's own dates. I need to split these apart with a precise, narrow query before I can tell Marco whether this €11.7k belongs in the leakage total, is a separate curiosity, or signals a real bug in the original orphan flag.

The good news from night 2: the incrementality re-cut (matched by item count) shows positive lift in every single bucket (+13% to +117%), which is a much stronger, more defensible signal than last week's confounded numbers — I'm now reasonably confident the top discounts are associated with genuinely bigger baskets, not just selection into already-large carts. And the tenant-by-half-year leakage breakdown confirms the 2024-peak/2025-decline pattern is broad-based across all 6 tenants, not one outlier fixing itself — so "slow-burning historical gap, now resolving" is a solid, well-checked claim for the memo. Neither needs more digging.

Tonight's two priorities: (1) cleanly split the 291 "unexplained" active-bucket orders into their true underlying cause (started-after-order vs. active-status-but-already-ended vs. a genuine bug in the original orphan flag), which determines the final €-figure I give Tobias; (2) check whether "subscription marked active/trialing/past_due but already has a past ended_at" is a one-off to these 6 tenants or a platform-wide data-quality issue, since that changes how I'd frame the finding and who else should know about it. I'm holding back a third slot rather than manufacturing a question — the other open items (incrementality, trend concentration, Welcome10 drivers) are already well-answered and I'd rather save the slot for whatever the diagnostic turns up.

input.notes:
Before writing anything near-final for Tobias, I need to flag something I should have caught earlier: the numbers across this whole investigation don't reconcile with each other. The original per-tenant orphan count for 2025 (night before last, summing Grind Collective 167 + Honeycomb Larder 127 + Kibblewick 100 + Feather & Fin 49 + Saffron & Sage 17 + The Balm Room 1 = 461 orders, €22,318.18 total) is far smaller than the "same population" reported a night later when split by subscription status (1,322 canceled + 291 active = 1,613 orders, €68,914.08 total) — a ~3.5x gap that I didn't catch before sending Friday's memo. And tonight's attempt to classify the 291 "active" orders by date logic came back internally inconsistent on its own terms: it reports 291 orders in one category but a discount total (€3,363.71) that matches a completely different, smaller 88-order subset from two nights ago — the count and the amount don't belong to the same population. Three different engineers independently "rebuilding the population from scratch" each night has clearly introduced drift (likely a 2025-only vs. full-history mismatch, and probably a join fan-out on the amount side).

I'm treating this as the priority for my last night: I'd rather hand Marco a number I've personally reconciled than compound a questionable one. All three requests tonight are single, self-contained, fan-out-safe queries that explicitly validate against previously-known, trusted reference totals, so I can see exactly where the drift is before writing anything definitive:
1. A single query, at tenant grain, for 2025 only, that reproduces last week's known-good per-tenant orphan totals (461 orders / €22,318.18) AND splits each tenant by subscription status in the same pass — so population and status-split can't drift apart.
2. The same construction extended to full history (2023-2025), checked against the monthly trend's cumulative total (~€57.7k for the canceled bucket, ~1,188 orders by my own hand-count of last week's monthly figures).
3. A careful, fan-out-safe rebuild of the date-logic classification for the active-bucket (started-after-order vs. active-but-already-ended vs. likely bug), built order-by-order first before aggregating, so the category counts and the discount total can't come from different populations.

I won't write the final headline number until I see these three agree with each other and with the known reference totals.

content.text:
# Memo: Promotions, Coupons & the Subscription-Leakage Number
**To:** Marco Bianchi | **From:** Oliver Grant | **Date:** Friday (Week 2)

## Findings

**1. Incrementality holds up under a harder test.** Controlling for basket size (number of distinct items, not price), discounted orders still show higher value than non-discounted orders of the *same* item count — lift ranges from +13% (3-item orders) to +117% (1-item orders), positive in all 5 size buckets (*"Incrementality re-cut: order value matched by basket size"*). This survives the strongest control we've applied. **Confidence: moderate-high** — still correlational (heavier spenders may simply be more likely to use codes), but no longer explained away by "coupons just land on bigger carts."

**2. Welcome10's refund pattern looks like normal apparel behavior, not abuse.** Returns are spread across many categories (Outerwear and Boots largest, ~19% of refund value each; no runaway concentration), with 9-19 day order-to-return gaps — classic fit/try-and-return timing, not quick-flip behavior. Combined with last week's finding that this merchant's baseline return rate is already ~37% with Welcome10 only +2.3pp above it, the "refund exceeds discount cost" framing is mostly mechanical for any % discount at a high-return apparel merchant, not something the coupon is causing. **Confidence: high.**

**3. The 6-tenant leakage story is real but I can't give you a trustworthy total yet.** This is the important one. Tonight's attempt to finalize last week's ~€57k lapsed-subscriber number instead surfaced a scope problem: a clean, twice-independently-confirmed figure exists for the *original 6 tenants*, 2025 only — **461 orphan orders, €22,318.18** (reconciled exactly in two separate reports tonight and three weeks ago). But the same reconciliation run also surfaced **6 additional tenants running the identical discount that were never in any prior week's analysis** — led by one tenant alone (891 orphan orders, €36,731.77) worth more than all 6 known tenants combined. Meanwhile, the query meant to validate the full-history (~€57.7k) trend came back **empty — wrong definition entirely** — and a sub-analysis of the "active-but-orphan" bucket has now given three different answers this week (88, then 291, then 560 orders) depending on which engineer rebuilt it from scratch. **Confidence: low on any total above €22.3k. I will not pass the €57k figure, or any larger revised figure, to Tobias as confirmed.**

## Caveats
- Every rebuild this week that said "same population as the prior report" was reconstructed from a text description, not the actual SQL — and each rebuild drifted. That's the root cause of #3.
- The full-history query tonight used a logically broken orphan definition and should be discarded, not read as "zero leakage historically."
- The newly discovered tenants weren't missing by accident of small size — one is bigger than our entire known population, which suggests our original "top 50 by cost" view genuinely never surfaced them, possibly a tenant-filter or page-cutoff issue worth checking in the original query too.

## Next steps
1. Before anything goes to Tobias: get the original "orphan population" SQL preserved verbatim and reused (not re-described) for every follow-up query — this alone would have prevented this week's drift.
2. Re-run the full tenant list (not assumed to be 6) for "Subscription delivery (prepaid)," 2025 and full history, with that one locked query.
3. Re-run the active-bucket date classification once, carefully, and treat the 88/291/560 results as unusable until then.
4. Keep #1 and #2 (incrementality, Welcome10) as-is for this week's readout — those are solid.
